definition: Signify means to be a sign of something — to stand for a meaning or make it known, often through a signal people have agreed to read the same way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word signify. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know signify should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: At the racetrack, a waved yellow flag signifies caution: hold your position, no passing, until the wreck ahead is cleared.
To hint is weaker than to signify: a hint gestures sideways at a meaning and can be missed or denied, while a sign that signifies carries its meaning plainly to everyone who knows the code.
Proclaim is stronger than signify: what a symbol quietly signifies to readers of the code, a proclamation announces outright — loudly, publicly, and to everyone at once.

Indicate is the everyday, instrumental verb for pointing something out or showing it — a gauge indicates speed and is done. Signify runs deeper: the sign carries a standing meaning, often by convention, the way a handshake signifies agreement.

Denote is the technical twin: a symbol denotes exactly what it is defined to mean and nothing more — the skull on the label denotes poison. Signify is broader and warmer, covering everything a gesture, mark, or event can mean to the people who read it.

The general's insignia caught the light as the honor guard passed the reviewing stand.
Signify means to be a sign of something — to stand for a meaning or make it known, often through a signal people have agreed to read the same way.

The linguistics professor opened the term with a dollar bill and a maple leaf: neither object resembles what it means, she said, yet one signifies value and the other signifies Canada, because communities have agreed to read them that way.
By the end of the hour the class was listing everything on campus that signified something — the bells, the robes, the unlocked quad gate.
To signify is to carry meaning for those who know the code.
The sign can be arbitrary — nothing about the color green means 'go' — but once the convention holds, the signal speaks by itself.
Carrying a standing, agreed meaning is what separates signifying from merely causing something or resembling it.
Signify is the workhorse for meaning-carrying: gestures, symbols, and events all signify.

Indicate is lighter and instrumental; denote is the logician's exact term; symbolize implies resemblance or association doing the work; portend and foreshadow, this unit's forward-looker, point specifically at what is to come, while signify marks a present meaning.
An older sense — 'it signifies little,' meaning it hardly matters — survives mostly in period fiction.
On the SAT you will often meet the word as 'signifies': same verb, third person.

On the trail crew, Maya's first lesson was about rock piles.
A stacked cairn does not just happen to sit beside the path; to everyone who works the ridge, it signifies the true route, especially in fog.
The stacks are a code the crews have kept for eighty years: one cairn for the route, two for a water source, a flat capstone for a dangerous drop ahead.
Hikers sometimes add decorative piles of their own, and the crew quietly unbuilds them, because a stack that means nothing weakens every stack that means something.
By August, Maya could read the ridge like a page -- each pile carrying its agreed meaning to anyone who knew the code.
